This course walks through the computational model of working memory used in the N-Back
fMRI study. Each lesson builds on the last, starting from first principles and ending
with a complete pipeline from raw behaviour to brain.

No prior knowledge of computational modelling is assumed, but familiarity with Python,
basic statistics, and the n-back task will help.

---

## Lessons

::: {.grid}

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### [Lesson 1 — Working Memory as a Decaying Buffer](lesson_01_memory_buffer.html)
Build the exponential decay buffer $A_k = \delta \cdot e^{-\mu k}$ from scratch.
Understand what $\delta$ (encoding amplitude) and $\mu$ (decay rate) mean, why the
buffer depth is capped at lag 10, and how lure effects emerge automatically without
any extra mechanism.

**Key concepts:** activation function · buffer data structure · δ as encoding probability
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### [Lesson 2 — From Activations to Decisions](lesson_02_decision_model.html)
Connect buffer activations to response probabilities via a probit decision model.
See why the model predicts elevated false alarms specifically on lure trials, how
β (criterion) and σ (noise) shape the psychometric function, and how α is identified
from the lure vs. novel non-match contrast.

**Key concepts:** SDT · probit model · trial-type predictions · α identifiability
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### [Lesson 3 — Interference, Normalisation, and Attentional Control](lesson_03_interference_control.html)
Build lure evidence $L$ and general interference $G$ from the buffer, understand why
normalising by total activation breaks the δ–σ confound, and derive the probit-normal
encoding-variance correction that handles Jensen's inequality without any extra parameters.

**Key concepts:** interference normalisation · δ–σ confound · probit-normal correction · why no proactive interference
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### [Lesson 4 — Fitting the Model](lesson_04_mle_model_comparison.html)
Fit parameters to behavioural data using maximum likelihood. Understand the parameter
transforms (logit/log) that keep optimisation unconstrained, why Nelder-Mead is used
instead of gradient methods, and how AIC/BIC selects M3 over four alternatives.

**Key concepts:** negative log-likelihood · parameter transforms · Nelder-Mead · AIC/BIC · boundary solutions
:::

::: {.g-col-12 .g-col-md-6}
### [Lesson 5 — From Parameters to Brain](lesson_05_fmri_regressors.html)
Use fitted parameters to generate trial-level parametric modulators for the fMRI GLM.
Build all five regressors (maintenance, control demand, lure activation, encoding
surprise, prediction error), z-score within run, inspect collinearity, and produce
FSL 3-column format files.

**Key concepts:** parametric modulators · regressor dissociation · z-scoring · FSL format
:::

:::
